sources.title: Why Zig When There Is Already C++, D, and Rust?
Introduction to Zig — Memory and Allocators

structure.rationale: The user's outline had 19 chapters across 5 parts, but they explicitly requested a small, to-the-point book with combined topics. This 8-chapter structure preserves every essential concept from the original outline while merging overlapping topics: ch1 covers philosophy and motivation, ch2 covers memory basics, ch3 the core interface, ch4-5 split stdlib allocators by usage pattern (general-purpose vs scoped), ch6 covers custom allocator design with a concrete bump allocator, ch7 merges the patterns/API-design chapters, and ch8 addresses performance and the decision framework. The order builds from why→what→how→apply.
structure.audience: Systems programmers (C/C++/Rust background) learning Zig, or Zig users who want deep allocator understanding.

claims.text: Zig's design principle: no hidden control flow, no hidden allocations. If a standard library function needs to allocate memory, it must receive an allocator as an argument.
There is no default global allocator in Zig. Functions that need to allocate memory accept an std.mem.Allocator parameter, making all heap allocations visible at the call site.
This design enables Zig code to be deployed in environments where a global allocator would be inappropriate: embedded systems, kernels, real-time systems, and WASM targets.

In contrast, C hides allocation behind malloc/free with no compile-time visibility; C++ hides it behind constructors, operator new, and STL defaults; Rust has a global allocator but ownership ensures safety; GC languages hide allocation entirely.
Zig's allocator-as-parameter pattern is a form of dependency injection: the caller decides the allocation strategy, not the callee.

snippets.note: Typical pattern: allocator passed as first parameter

pitfalls: Beginners from GC languages expect allocation to 'just work' — the explicit allocator is an adjustment.

claims.text: Stack memory in Zig is managed automatically by the compiler. Local variables live on the stack frame and are freed when the function returns. Stack size is typically 8MB on Linux.
Heap memory requires explicit allocation via an allocator and explicit deallocation (or bulk deallocation via arena). The heap is managed through OS-level calls (mmap, VirtualAlloc).

Alignment in Zig is a first-class concept. Every pointer type carries an alignment: *align(N) T. The allocator interface respects alignment requirements. Common alignments: 1 for u8, 4 for u32, 8 for u64, 16 for SIMD types.
Zig uses usize for sizes and pointer arithmetic. anyopaque is the type-erased pointer (equivalent to C's void*).
Allocators in Zig return error unions (!T): allocation can fail, and the error must be handled. This contrasts with C's malloc returning null and C++'s new throwing.

The defer keyword ensures cleanup runs when the scope exits, regardless of how (return, error, etc.). errdefer runs only on error paths — essential for allocator cleanup in functions that might fail after allocating.

pitfalls: Forgetting errdefer when a function can fail after allocating leads to leaks on error paths.
Stack-allocated slices cannot escape their function — returning a pointer to a local is a compile error.

claims.text: std.mem.Allocator is a two-field struct: ptr (*anyopaque, the allocator's own state) and vtable (*const VTable, the method dispatch table). This gives runtime polymorphism without generics overhead.

The VTable defines four function pointers: alloc (allocate new memory), resize (try to resize in place without moving), remap (resize, possibly relocating), and free (release memory). All take alignment as a log2 value.
The high-level convenience methods on Allocator — create(), destroy(), alloc(), realloc(), free(), dupe(), dupeZ() — all delegate to the VTable's four primitives.
create(T) allocates a single value of type T and returns *T. alloc(T, n) allocates a slice []T of n elements. Both respect T's alignment automatically.
resize() returns a bool: true if it could resize in place, false otherwise. This is a hint to the allocator — it never moves memory. realloc() may move memory if resize fails.
The allocator interface is passed by value (it's two pointers, 16 bytes). This is intentional: it makes the interface cheap to pass and avoids lifetime concerns about the interface struct itself.

snippets.note: Simplified Allocator struct and VTable (actual has more parameters)

pitfalls: Mismatching alloc/free with different allocators is undefined behavior.
The ret_addr parameter is for debug stack traces — pass @returnAddress() when implementing.

claims.text: std.heap.page_allocator: the most basic allocator, wraps OS page allocation (mmap on Linux, VirtualAlloc on Windows). Allocates in page-sized chunks (typically 4096 bytes). Slow and wasteful for small allocations, but the simplest and most portable.

std.heap.GeneralPurposeAllocator (GPA, renamed to DebugAllocator in recent Zig): a configurable safety-first allocator. In debug/safe modes it detects double-free, use-after-free, and memory leaks. In release modes it's a straightforward general-purpose allocator.

GPA configuration options include: .safety (enable/disable safety checks), .never_unmap (keep freed pages mapped for use-after-free detection), .stack_trace_frames (number of stack frames to capture per allocation for leak reports).
GPA.deinit() returns a status indicating whether any memory was leaked. Idiomatic pattern: 'const check = gpa.deinit(); if (check == .leak) @panic("leaked");'
std.heap.c_allocator: wraps C's malloc/free/realloc. Only available when linking against libc. Useful for C interop — when passing memory across FFI boundaries that the C side will free.
std.testing.allocator: a wrapper that fails the test if any memory is leaked. All standard library tests use it. It's GPA-backed with mandatory leak checking.
std.heap.LoggingAllocator: a wrapper that logs every alloc/resize/free to a writer. Useful for understanding allocation patterns in a program.

snippets.note: GPA setup with leak checking on deinit

pitfalls: GPA is not the fastest allocator — it's designed for safety. Use it during development, consider alternatives for hot paths in production.
page_allocator wastes memory for small allocations (a 1-byte alloc still consumes a 4096-byte page).

claims.text: std.heap.ArenaAllocator: wraps a child allocator. Individual free() calls are no-ops. All memory is released at once via deinit() or reset(). Internally it chains pages from the child allocator and bump-allocates within them.
Arena is ideal for phase-scoped memory: per-request handling in a server, per-frame in a game, per-pass in a compiler. The pattern is: create arena at scope start, use it freely, deinit at scope end.
ArenaAllocator.reset() modes: .retain (keep all pages allocated for reuse — fast for repeated phases), .free_all (return all pages to the child allocator).

std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator: allocates from a caller-provided byte slice. No heap allocation at all. Returns error.OutOfMemory when the buffer is exhausted. Individual free() calls mark memory as reusable.
FixedBufferAllocator is essential for embedded systems, kernel code, and any context where heap allocation is forbidden. It can also be used with stack-allocated buffers for fast, bounded allocation.

Composing allocators: ArenaAllocator(page_allocator) is the most common composition — the arena amortizes page-granularity cost across many small allocations. ArenaAllocator(FixedBufferAllocator) creates a bounded arena.

snippets.note: Arena pattern: allocate many, free once

pitfalls: Arena allocations cannot be individually freed — if one allocation must be freed early, an arena is the wrong tool.
FixedBufferAllocator silently fails (returns error) when exhausted — size the buffer carefully.

claims.text: To implement a custom allocator, define a struct with your allocator's state, implement the four VTable functions (alloc, resize, remap, free), create a const VTable instance, and expose an allocator() method that returns std.mem.Allocator{ .ptr = self, .vtable = &vtable }.

A bump (linear) allocator is the simplest useful custom allocator: maintain a pointer into a pre-allocated buffer that advances on each allocation. Reset returns the pointer to the start. Individual frees are no-ops or unsupported.
Alignment must be handled explicitly: round the current offset up to the requested alignment before advancing the pointer. Zig provides std.mem.alignForward for this.

The ret_addr parameter (return address) in VTable functions is for debug tooling — it lets allocators record where each allocation was made, enabling useful leak reports. Pass @returnAddress() when calling through.

A pool (slab) allocator pre-divides memory into fixed-size blocks and maintains a free list. Allocation is O(1) (pop from free list), as is deallocation (push to free list). Ideal for allocating many objects of the same type.

Testing custom allocators: use std.testing.allocator as a reference, write tests that allocate/free/resize and check invariants. The FailingAllocator can simulate allocation failures for robustness testing.

pitfalls: Forgetting alignment leads to bus errors or silent data corruption on architectures with strict alignment requirements.
A bump allocator that doesn't support free leaks memory in long-running programs — only use for bounded scopes.

claims.text: Zig's standard data structures (ArrayList, HashMap, BufMap, etc.) all accept an allocator parameter in their init functions. This is the allocator-aware container pattern — the container doesn't choose its allocation strategy, the user does.
API design rule: if your function or struct allocates, accept an Allocator parameter. If it doesn't allocate, don't. This is a signal to the caller about what the function does.

Wrapper/composition pattern: LoggingAllocator, FailingAllocator, and custom wrappers that add behavior (metrics, quotas, tracing) around a child allocator. Each wrapper implements the Allocator interface and delegates to the child.
Per-subsystem allocators: give each major subsystem its own allocator. This makes it possible to track per-subsystem memory usage, apply different strategies, and tear down subsystem memory in bulk.
The 'temporary + permanent' pattern: use an arena for scratch work (parsing, intermediate results) and a GPA for long-lived data. The arena is reset each cycle; the GPA catches any permanent leaks.

C interop: use c_allocator when passing memory to C code that will call free(). Use a Zig allocator when the memory stays Zig-managed. Never mix: memory allocated by one allocator must be freed by the same one.

snippets.note: Per-request arena in a server loop

pitfalls: Mixing allocators (allocating with one, freeing with another) is undefined behavior and often silent.
Storing an arena-allocated pointer in a struct that outlives the arena is a dangling pointer bug.

claims.text: Allocator performance varies by orders of magnitude: page_allocator involves a syscall per allocation (~microseconds), GPA uses buckets (~hundreds of nanoseconds), arena is a pointer bump (~nanoseconds), FixedBufferAllocator is a pointer bump with no syscall.
For performance-critical paths: measure first, then switch allocators. A LoggingAllocator or custom instrumentation can reveal how many allocations a hot loop makes, their sizes, and lifetimes.

Fragmentation: page_allocator has no fragmentation (whole pages). GPA can fragment over time with mixed-size allocations. Arena has no fragmentation within a phase. Pool allocators have no fragmentation for their fixed block size.

Embedded/kernel: FixedBufferAllocator or a custom pool allocator. No syscalls, bounded memory, deterministic behavior. The allocator pattern itself has zero overhead — it's two pointers and a vtable call.

Decision framework: development → GPA (catches bugs). Short-lived scratch → arena. Fixed-count objects → pool. No heap allowed → FixedBufferAllocator. C interop → c_allocator. Production general-purpose → GPA in ReleaseFast or a tuned arena.
Thread safety: most standard allocators are NOT thread-safe by default. For multi-threaded use, use std.heap.ThreadSafeAllocator wrapper or per-thread allocators.

pitfalls: Premature allocator optimization: switching from GPA to a raw arena removes safety checks. Keep GPA in debug builds.
Assuming all allocators are thread-safe — they're not by default.
